newsitem.title: INDONESIA: East Timor poll-related death toll rises to 17.
newsitem.headline: East Timor poll-related death toll rises to 17.

text.p: The number of people killed in poll-related violence in East Timor rose to 17, but calm had generally returned to the former Portuguese colony on Friday after separatist protests whipped up by Indonesia's general elections.

The number of civilians shot dead by separatist guerrillas in the town of Los Palos, about 200 km (124 miles) east of Dili rose to eight, from seven, said the territory's police chief, Colonel Yusuf Muharam. The shooting occurred late on Wednesday, and the guerrillas took three hostages.
"Soldiers managed to free two of the hostages on Thursday but the third was shot dead by the guerrillas," Muharam said.
He said three guerrillas were killed on Wednesday night in an attack by about 20 dissidents on a riot police post on the Dili outskirts. Four soldiers were wounded.

"They were armed with very old M-16 rifles and were continuing to return our fire," he said. "We chased after them up the hills and on Thursday morning arrested two. A few hours later we shot dead one more and injured another."
The wounded man later died, he said.
Police and residents said the capital Dili and most other areas were relatively calm on Friday after voting on Thursday for a national parliament and regional and local assemblies.

In East Timor's second city of Baucau, two civilians were shot dead on Wednesday night by guerrillas, Muharam said. On Thursday, a soldier guarding a polling place in Ermera district was shot dead by separatists attempting to destroy the booth. A resident in Dili contacted by phone said the situation there and most of East Timor was calm on Friday.
"The situation is returning to normal after yesterday's voting," he said.

Diplomats said separatists had wanted demonstrate their strength in East Timor, which Indonesia occupied in 1975 and annexed the next year, and the result was the worst fatal violence in the territory in years.

The United Nations still refuses to recognise Indonesia's sovereignty over East Timor, and Portugal said on Thursday it had protested to the world body over the elections. The Indonesian military, which maintains a strong presence in East Timor, says about 80 poorly-armed guerrillas remain in the rugged hills. Other sources suggest there are around 200.

Election figures released at 10:30 a.m. (0330 GMT) on Friday showed Indonesia's ruling Golkar -- experiencing a landslide elsewhere in the country -- had taken 84.4 percent of the votes counted in the mainly-Catholic territory.

The Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), swamped elsewhere, had 13.4 percent. The Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) had just over two percent. In the remote eastern island of Flores, meanwhile, hundreds of people protested in two villages after election officials said Golkar had won all the votes, residents said.
"In Sinar Hading village, almost 300 voters were angry when the election committee announced that Golkar got 100 percent of the vote," one resident told Reuters by telephone.
"They demaded a recount which saw Golkar only getting 292 of the 409 votes cast," he said.
In Ile Padung village, 13 people were detained but released hours later on Thursday after they protested against the result of the vote count.
